Series::cov¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::cov() const
Series Series::cov(std::int64_t correction) const

What It Does¶

Builds the covariance matrix of a set of variables.

Covariance measures how two quantities move together. If a variable is centered (its mean subtracted), the average product of two centered variables is their covariance: large and positive when they rise and fall in step, large and negative when one rises as the other falls, near zero when they are unrelated. cov() computes that number for every pair of variables at once and lays the results out in a square matrix.

The layout convention is the part to get right:

  • a 2-D input is read as one variable per row, observed across the columns. A [V, N] input is V variables with N observations each, and cov() returns a [V, V] matrix whose (i, j) entry is the covariance of variable i with variable j.

  • a 1-D input is a single variable, and cov() returns its scalar variance.

The diagonal of the matrix is each variable’s own variance (a variable’s covariance with itself). The matrix is always symmetric: entry (i, j) equals entry (j, i).

Internally each row is centered with center and the matrix is formed as Xc @ Xc^T divided by N - correction, all on the differentiable path, so cov() can sit inside an objective you optimize.

Parameters¶

correction (std::int64_t, default 1): the divisor is num_observations - correction.

  • correction = 1 (the default) is the sample covariance — the unbiased estimator, dividing by N - 1.

  • correction = 0 is the population covariance, dividing by N.

Any integer is accepted; N - correction <= 0 yields non-finite entries.

Returns¶

Series For a [V, N] input, a [V, V] symmetric covariance matrix in float64. For a 1-D input, a float64 scalar variance. Integer inputs are promoted to float64 first.

Gradient¶

Differentiable. The centering and the Xc @ Xc^T product are both on the taped path, so an objective built through cov() (a risk penalty, a decorrelation loss, a whitening term) propagates sensitivities back to the data.

Examples¶

Example 1. Two variables, four observations each. Rows are the variables.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0},
                             {1.0, 3.0, 5.0, 8.0}});
std::cout << x.cov();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[1.6666667, 3.8333333],
  [3.8333333, 8.9166667]]

The (0, 1) and (1, 0) entries are equal — covariance is symmetric. Both are positive here because the two rows increase together.

Example 2. A 1-D input is one variable, so cov() is its scalar variance.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 4.0, 4.0, 5.0, 5.0, 7.0, 9.0}).cov();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=4.5714286

The mean is 5; the squared deviations sum to 32; 32 / (8 - 1) = 4.571....

Example 3. correction sets the divisor. The default divides by N - 1; correction = 0 divides by N.

auto x = pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 4.0, 4.0, 5.0, 5.0, 7.0, 9.0});
std::cout << "N-1: " << x.cov();
std::cout << "N  : " << x.cov(0);

Output¶

N-1: pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=4.5714286N  : pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=4

32 / 8 = 4 exactly. The N - 1 form is larger — it inflates the estimate to correct for the bias of using the sample mean.

Example 4. The diagonal is exactly each row’s variance.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0},
                             {1.0, 3.0, 5.0, 8.0}});
std::cout << "cov diag = " << x.cov().diagonal();
std::cout << "row0 var = " << x.slice(0, 0, 1).reshape({4}).var();
std::cout << "row1 var = " << x.slice(0, 1, 2).reshape({4}).var();

Output¶

cov diag = pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1.6666667, 8.9166667]row0 var = pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[1.6666667]row1 var = pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[8.9166667]

var also defaults to the N - 1 divisor, so the numbers line up.

Example 5. The matrix is symmetric — C minus its transpose is all zero.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0},
                             {2.0, 1.0, 4.0, 3.0},
                             {5.0, 6.0, 5.0, 6.0}});
auto c = x.cov();
std::cout << c;
std::cout << "max|C - C^T| = " << c.sub(c.transpose(0, 1)).abs().max();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=9, contiguous=true)
data=[[1.6666667, 1, 0.33333333],
  [1, 1.6666667, -0.33333333],
  [0.33333333, -0.33333333, 0.33333333]]max|C - C^T| = pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=0

Three variables give a 3 x 3 matrix. The third row is nearly constant, so its variance (0.333) is small.

Example 6. Gradient flows: cov() is on the differentiable path.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0},
                             {1.0, 3.0, 5.0, 8.0}});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.cov().sum().reverse();
std::cout << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=8, contiguous=true)
data=[[-3.1666667, -1.1666667, 0.83333333, 3.5],
  [-3.1666667, -1.1666667, 0.83333333, 3.5]]

The sensitivity of sum(cov(X)) to observation j is proportional to the sum, across variables, of that observation’s centered value — which is why both rows receive the same gradient here.

Example 7. Two variables that move in opposite directions have a negative off-diagonal.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0},
                             {4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0}});
std::cout << x.cov();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[1.6666667, -1.6666667],
  [-1.6666667, 1.6666667]]

The rows are exact mirror images, so the off-diagonal is -1 times the shared variance. The diagonal is unchanged — variance never sees the sign.

Example 8. Three or more dimensions are rejected.

try {
  std::cout << pluss::series::zeros({2, 2, 2}).cov();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

cov: expected a 1D or 2D input

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Rows are variables, columns are observations. If your data is stored the other way (one row per observation), transpose it first: x.transpose(0, 1).cov(). Getting this backwards silently computes the covariance of the wrong thing.

  • The default divisor is N - 1, not N. Pass cov(0) for the population form. This matches var and std.

  • With a single observation (N = 1) the default divisor is 0 and every entry is non-finite.

  • NaN in any observation propagates through the centering and the product, so one missing value can poison an entire row and column of the result. Filter or impute first.

  • The result is always float64. An integer input is promoted; it is not kept integral.

  • cov() does not weight observations. For a weighted covariance, scale the centered data yourself.

Summary¶

cov() is the covariance matrix of a set of variables:

  • 2-D input: one variable per row, [V, N] in, [V, V] symmetric matrix out

  • 1-D input: a single variable, scalar variance out

  • diagonal entries are each variable’s variance

  • divisor is N - correction; correction = 1 (default) is the unbiased sample form, correction = 0 the population form

  • differentiable; float64 result

See Also¶

  • Series::corrcoef: cov() rescaled so the diagonal is 1 and every entry lies in [-1, 1] — covariance with the units divided out.

  • Series::var / Series::std: the single-variable spread; the diagonal of cov().

  • Series::center: subtract the mean — the first step cov() performs internally.

  • Series::outer: the un-centered, un-scaled rank-1 product that cov() generalizes.
